passages.title: Watching, reproducing and choosing to do it again
paragraphs: Children acquire a great deal without ever being reinforced for it, simply by watching what someone else does and what happens next. To separate what a child takes in from what a child is willing to perform, investigators built a task no child could already know: a twelve-step assembly in which coloured blocks had to be fitted into a frame in a fixed order. One hundred and twenty children aged 7 to 9 were recruited from four after-school clubs and assigned at random to one of four conditions, thirty per condition. Three conditions watched the same three-minute video of an adult completing the assembly correctly. In the first, the adult was then praised warmly by a second adult; in the second nothing was said; in the third the adult was told the work was careless and would not count. The fourth condition saw no video and was simply shown the blocks and the frame.

Immediately afterwards each child was taken to a separate room, given the blocks, and asked to build whatever they could. A scorer who did not know the condition recorded how many of the twelve steps were produced in the correct order. Two days later the same children spent twenty minutes in a playroom that held the blocks among eight other activities, and an observer recorded whether the child picked up the blocks at all. Table 1 gives the means and the proportion who did so.

Reproduction was similar in all three conditions that saw the model, and in all three far above the condition that did not. Free-choice behaviour behaved quite differently. Children who had seen the model criticised reproduced 8.7 steps, within 0.9 of the children who had seen the model praised, yet were only three-eighths as likely to touch the blocks when nothing was asked of them. The investigators argued that a consequence delivered to someone else does not much change what an observer takes in; what it changes is the observer's estimate of what the behaviour is worth doing.

passages.title: Two kinds of remembering after hippocampal injury
paragraphs: Memory is not one faculty. One kind supports statements a person can make about facts and events and can be brought deliberately to mind; another supports skills and habits and shows itself only in performance. Nine adults who had sustained bilateral damage to the hippocampus and the cortex adjacent to it, following a period of oxygen deprivation, were compared with nine volunteers matched to them individually for age, years of schooling and vocabulary score. All nine patients were severely impaired in daily life at remembering conversations and appointments. None had difficulty with speech, with naming, or with general knowledge acquired before the injury.

Four tasks were given on each of five consecutive days. Free recall required the participant to study a list of twenty unrelated words and then produce as many as possible. Recognition required a yes-or-no judgement on forty studied pictures mixed with forty new ones. Mirror tracing required the participant to trace a six-pointed star while seeing the hand only in a mirror, and errors were counted each day. Stem completion presented thirty three-letter stems, each of which had begun a word studied an hour earlier, and the measure was the proportion completed with the studied word; a separate set of stems whose words had not been studied gave a baseline rate. Table 1 gives the group means.

The two groups diverged sharply on the tasks that asked for a deliberate report and barely at all on the others. Both groups cut their tracing errors by about two thirds over the five days. The patients completed primed stems with a studied word nearly four times as often as their own unprimed baseline rate, a difference as large as the controls'. Asked on day five whether they had traced the star before, eight of the nine patients said they had not, and two asked what the mirror was for.

passages.title: Disparity, convergence and judged distance in the dark
paragraphs: Two eyes set a few centimetres apart receive slightly different images of anything nearer than the horizon, and the difference between those images, the binocular disparity, shrinks as an object recedes. The angle through which the eyes must turn inward to fixate an object, the convergence angle, shrinks with distance in the same way. Both therefore carry information about depth that is useful nearby and almost useless far off. To find how much of a distance judgement rests on them, investigators tested sixty-four adults in a blacked-out room containing a single small light-emitting diode on a movable track, with every other cue to depth removed.

Each participant judged the distance to the diode, in metres, at five actual distances, in each of three viewing conditions presented in a counterbalanced order. In binocular viewing both eyes were open. In monocular viewing the non-dominant eye was patched. In the third condition both eyes were open but each looked through a weak prism that halved the disparity between the two retinal images while leaving the convergence demand almost unchanged. Figure 1 plots the mean judged distance in each condition against the actual distance, on a logarithmic horizontal axis, together with a thin dashed curve marking judgements that would be exactly correct.

Binocular judgements were essentially correct within about a metre and fell progressively short of the diode's true distance beyond that. Monocular judgements overestimated the nearest distance almost threefold and fell further short than binocular judgements at the far end of the range. The prism condition lay nearer the monocular curve than the binocular curve at every distance. The investigators concluded that the near advantage of two eyes over one rests chiefly on disparity rather than on convergence, and that at eight metres no viewing condition was accurate, because the cues that help nearby have little left to contribute there.

passages.title: Rewarding an activity children had already chosen
paragraphs: Some activities are undertaken for their own sake, and a standing question is what happens to such an activity once it is also paid for. From three weeks of unobtrusive observation in nine nursery classrooms, investigators identified ninety children aged 4 and 5 who spent a high proportion of free-choice time drawing. During a baseline week each child's drawing was timed across a single twenty-minute free-choice period in which drawing was one of six available activities.

In the following week each child was taken individually to a side room and invited to draw for six minutes. Thirty children, chosen at random, were told before they began that anyone who drew would receive a Good Artist certificate, and were given one afterwards. Thirty were told nothing beforehand and were given the same certificate afterwards, with no explanation of why. Thirty were told nothing and given nothing. A week later, drawing was timed again in the same twenty-minute free-choice period. The observers who timed the free-choice periods did not know which child had been in which group. Table 1 gives the means.

Drawing in the group that had expected the certificate halved. The two other groups were essentially unchanged. The investigators argued that what matters is not whether a reward arrives but whether the child can treat it as the reason for drawing: a certificate announced in advance supplies a ready external reason, while one that arrives unannounced does not, because the drawing is finished before the certificate exists. Nothing in the design bears on how long the change lasts, and all ninety children were selected because they already drew a great deal, so the result says nothing about children indifferent to drawing.

passages.title: Building and checking a five-factor inventory
paragraphs: A personality inventory is useful only if its items hang together, if they give similar scores on two occasions, and if they agree with something other than the respondent's own report. Investigators wrote 180 self-descriptive statements, administered them to 600 adults recruited from an online panel, and discarded every item that correlated poorly with the rest or that almost everyone endorsed. Sixty items survived. A factor analysis of the correlations among those sixty items returned five factors, and every item loaded most strongly on exactly one of them. The five were labelled, by inspection of their highest-loading items, as extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, emotional stability and openness.

Each factor was scored as the mean of its items, and internal consistency was computed within each scale. Four hundred and eighty of the 600 respondents completed the inventory again eight weeks later, and the correlation between the two administrations gives the retest figure. Each respondent also nominated one friend of at least two years' standing, who rated the respondent on the same sixty statements reworded in the third person; 412 friends returned usable ratings. Table 1 reports, for each factor, the number of items, the percentage of the total item variance it accounted for, the internal consistency, the eight-week retest correlation, and the correlation between self-report and friend report.

The five factors together accounted for 54 percent of the variance in the sixty items, leaving almost half of it unaccounted for. Internal consistency and retest stability were comparable across the five scales. Self-friend agreement was not: it ran from 0.54 for extraversion down to 0.33 for emotional stability. The investigators observed that the scales on which friends agreed least are the ones whose defining statements refer to states that are mostly not visible from outside, and that a low self-friend correlation is therefore ambiguous between an inaccurate self-report and an uninformed friend.

passages.title: A habit of explanation and the first episode of low mood
paragraphs: Two people meeting the same setback explain it differently. One treats it as a passing matter with a local cause; the other treats it as evidence of something stable in themselves that will spoil other things too. The second habit of explanation is what is meant by a negative attributional style, and the proposal under test is that it is not merely a symptom of low mood but a standing vulnerability that shows itself when something goes wrong. Investigators administered a 24-item measure of attributional style to 1,340 students entering a single university, and screened all of them with a structured diagnostic interview. Students who met criteria for a current or a past depressive episode were excluded, which left 480.

The 480 were divided at the median of the attributional-style score into a high-risk and a low-risk half of 240 each, and followed for 18 months. Every six months a diagnostic interview, conducted by an interviewer who did not know the student's attributional score, recorded whether a first major depressive episode had begun. At each interview students also reported whether any of eleven listed major stressors, such as a bereavement, a serious illness or the end of a long relationship, had occurred since the previous interview. Table 1 gives the number of first episodes, overall and by whether a major stressor had been reported.

The high-risk half were more than twice as likely as the low-risk half to have a first episode, with incidences of 20.0 and 7.5 percent and a relative risk of 2.67. Dividing by stressor exposure shows where that difference sat. Among students reporting a major stressor the two halves differed by 17.5 percentage points; among those reporting none they differed by 7.8 points. The investigators read this as a diathesis-stress pattern. They were careful to note that attributional style was not assigned, and that the median split was fixed before any outcome was known.

passages.title: Fifteen minutes of discussion and the drift of a committee
paragraphs: A committee that talks often ends up more extreme than its members were when they sat down. To test whether discussion itself produces the drift, investigators recruited 150 adults and had each read a short scenario in which a manager must decide whether to commit a firm's reserves to an untested product. Each rated privately how acceptable the commitment was, on a nine-point scale where 1 was wholly unacceptable and 9 wholly acceptable. From those ratings the investigators formed thirty groups of five, each composed so that all five members had rated the scenario on the same side of the midpoint: fifteen groups of members leaning toward accepting the risk, and fifteen of members leaning toward caution.

Groups of each kind were then assigned at random either to discuss the scenario for fifteen minutes, reaching no formal decision, or to spend the same fifteen minutes re-reading the scenario in silence in the same room. Afterwards every participant rated the scenario again, privately and without consulting anyone. Table 1 gives the mean rating before and after, by group type and condition, averaged over the members of the groups in each cell.

Discussion moved each kind of group about a full point further in the direction its members already leaned, so that the two kinds ended further apart than they began. Groups that merely re-read the scenario moved a tenth of a point. Because membership was composed from the pre-discussion ratings, no group contained a member arguing the other side, and the investigators noted that their design therefore says nothing about what discussion does to a group divided at the outset.

passages.title: Which voices carry a norm to an adolescent
paragraphs: Norms reach a young person by more than one route, and the routes can be told apart. An injunctive norm is a belief about what other people would approve or disapprove of. A descriptive norm is a belief about what other people in fact do. Investigators surveyed 1,200 adolescents aged 14 to 17, sampled from the enrolment registers of 48 secondary schools in one country. Each was asked how wrong it would be for an adult to understate their income on a tax return, on a five-point scale from not wrong at all to very seriously wrong. That rating was the study's outcome.

Five predictors were measured. Parental disapproval and peer disapproval were each the adolescent's report of how strongly their parents, and separately their closest friends, would disapprove of understating income. Perceived prevalence was the adolescent's estimate of the percentage of adults in their own community who understate income. Civics instruction was the number of hours of formal teaching on taxation and public spending that the adolescent's school reported for the year. Hours per week spent watching a popular television drama about a corrupt business family were recorded as the fifth. All five entered a single regression, with age, sex and household income held constant. Table 1 gives the standardised coefficients.

The two injunctive measures were the strongest predictors, and the descriptive measure ran the other way: an adolescent who believed that most adults understate income rated the practice as less seriously wrong. The model accounted for 24 percent of the variance in the ratings. The investigators observed that every predictor except the two drawn from school and viewing records is a report given by the adolescent, that none was manipulated, and that an adolescent who already thinks the practice trivial may also report lenient parents.

passages.title: Who is counted as working, and who is working
paragraphs: Participation in the paid labour force is counted as being either employed or actively seeking work. In most national statistics the participation rates of men and of women differ little among adults without dependent children and widely among those with them. A national household survey of one middle-income country interviewed 40,000 adults aged 25 to 54 and classified each by sex and by the age of the youngest child in the household. Respondents who were employed were also asked to account for a typical week in two parts: hours of paid work, and hours of unpaid household and care work.

Table 1 gives the participation rates. The gap between men and women is 7 percentage points among adults with no child under 18, 16 points where the youngest child is of school age, and 32 points where the youngest is under 6, which is more than four times the gap among adults with no child under 18. Men's participation is, if anything, slightly higher among fathers of young children than among men with no children at all.

Among those employed, men reported 41 hours of paid work and 14 hours of unpaid household and care work in a typical week; women reported 33 and 26. The two sexes therefore reported similar totals, 55 hours against 59, distributed very differently between work that the participation statistics count and work that they do not. The survey recorded nothing about whether respondents would have preferred a different arrangement, and a rate measured at a single moment cannot distinguish a woman who has left the labour force for good from one who intends to return.

passages.title: Sixty years of births, deaths and cities
paragraphs: In the demographic transition a population moves from high birth and death rates to low ones, but not simultaneously. Mortality falls first, and for a time births continue at close to their former rate, so a population grows fastest in the middle of the transition rather than at either end. Urban growth has sources of its own: natural increase within cities, migration from the countryside, and the reclassification of settlements that have grown past a statistical threshold. A country can therefore urbanise quickly while its rate of natural increase is falling. Table 1 gives sixty years of registration and census data for one middle-income country.

The crude death rate halved between 1960 and 1980, from 24 to 12 per thousand, while the crude birth rate fell by less than a seventh over the same two decades. Natural increase therefore peaked in 1980 at 26 per thousand. Over the following forty years the birth rate fell by more than half and natural increase fell with it, reaching 7 per thousand by 2020. The death rate did not continue to fall after 1980, because the population was ageing, and an older population raises the crude death rate even where mortality at any given age is still improving.

The urban share rose in every period, from 18 percent to 68 percent. Because the total population also more than tripled, the number of people living in urban areas grew by much more than the rise in the share alone suggests. The census does not separate the three sources of urban growth, so these figures cannot say how much of the increase was migration from the countryside and how much was births to people already living in cities.
